newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks plummet, biggest point drop since 1987.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks plummet, biggest point drop since 1987.

text.p: U.S. blue-chip stocks plunged on Friday, posting their biggest point drop since the 1987 stock market crash in a sell-off sparked by a weakening dollar and worries about corporate earnings.
Bond prices recovered after an early fall.
The Dow Jones industrial average tumbled 247.37 points, or 3.1 percent, at 7,694.66, marking its second-biggest point drop ever. Friday's slide puts the index at its lowest close since June.

The blue-chip market also suffered its worst week ever, beating the weekly trading period that included the so-called Black Monday stock market crash on Oct. 19, 1987. On that day, the Dow sank 508 points, or 23 percent, to 1,738.74.
The loss for this week of 336.56 points was the worst decline in history. But in percentage terms, the sell-off was not among the top 10 weekly declines.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 2,116 to 714 on an active volume of 534 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
With the loss, the Dow has fallen 6.8 percent from its all-time closing high of 8,259.31, set on Aug. 6.
The market suffered a case of the nerves at the opening bell, with the Dow falling more than 100 points in the first few minutes of trading.

Traders were rattled after Gillette Co. told analysts it expects disappointing 1997 earnings. On the heels of a similar warnings from Coca-Cola Co. earlier this month, this sparked considerable worry about corporate America's future profits.
Adding to the day's volatility was the "double-witching" expiration of options on stocks and stock indexes.
Analysts believed that the market's slide was not the signal of the beginning of a bear market, though some said they had noticed a distinct shift in the mood on Wall Street.

"We're witnessing a transition from buy on weakness to sell on strength ... and it wouldn't surprise me if what we're seeing is the footsteps of some program trading," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management.
He said the raging bullishness that was the hallmark of July's stock market no longer had the support of lower bond interest rates.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond edged up 1/32, or 31 cents on a $1,000 bond, leaving its yield unchanged at 6.55 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
While the long-bond rate has come down from a recent peak of 6.70 percent, it is still one-quarter point higher than the 6.33 percent rate on July 30, when the Dow stood at a then-record 8,254.89.
Analysts said the market fall was exaggerated because many traders were not at work on a summer Friday afternoon, so fewer buyers were around to step in on the weakness.
Last Friday, stocks were also clobbered with the Dow dropping 156 points.
Consumer products stocks took it on the chin after Gillette's warning. Gillette slumped 4-5/16 to close at 85-7/8 and Procter & Gamble Co. lost 7-1/2 to 136-9/16.

Mounting speculation that Germany will raise interest rates when it returns from summer recess next week drove the dollar down against the mark. The dollar fell to 1.8205 marks from 1.8395 marks at Thursday's close.

Falling stocks helped to boost gold prices, but the gains were limited by the drop in the dollar. At the Commodity Exchange in New York, gold for December delivery rose $1.50 to close at $329.50 an ounce.
Overseas, Britain's FTSE 100 fell 125.5 points, or 2.51 percent, to 4,865.8. In Tokyo, the 225-stock Nikkei average rose 103.41 points, or 0.54 percent, to 19,326.03.
